cards.title: Query fan-out: why AI citation needs topical coverage, not one keyword
cards.summary: AI assistants expand a single prompt into many synthetic sub-queries, so you must be relevant across a whole topic rather than one head keyword.
cards.use_when: Planning product-category content or PDP/editorial coverage and deciding which topics to own so your products can be surfaced inside AI answers.
steps: Treat an AI prompt as a research brief, not a lookup: the assistant breaks it into dozens of narrower questions and runs them in parallel, then synthesizes the results. The source cites a reported example of ChatGPT's deep research mode running 420 searches for a prompt about buying a red phone case.

Map the sub-queries a real buyer's prompt implies. Example from the source: 'Plan me a five-day trip to Japan in November' fans out to 'best neighborhoods to stay in Tokyo,' 'November weather in Kyoto,' 'is the Japan Rail Pass worth it.'

For ecommerce, apply this by covering the comparison, fit, use-case and objection questions behind a category (e.g., material durability, sizing, compatibility, vs-alternatives) on category pages, buying guides and PDPs.

Recognize the three retrieval-probability factors the source cites from Ahrefs research: consensus (same brand claims repeated across many places), freshness (AI-cited content averaged ~25.7% fresher than top Google results), and authority (76% of AI overview citations came from pages already in Google's top 10).
Conclude that traditional SEO is the foundation; if you already rank top-10 on Google you start with an advantage.
Prioritize building relevance across the full topic cluster rather than optimizing single keywords.
caveats: The 420-search figure was a reported example, not a guaranteed depth per query.
Freshness/authority percentages are Ahrefs research findings cited by the presenter, not universal guarantees.

cards.title: Brand gap analysis to find missed AI citations
cards.summary: Run a brand gap analysis to surface where your brand is mentioned-but-not-cited, where competitors win, and which topics AI associates with others.
cards.use_when: Auditing AI visibility before choosing which ecommerce content, PDP or mention-building work to do next.
steps: Measure where your brand should appear versus where it actually appears across Google, AI results and the web. The source suggests a tool like Ahrefs Brand Radar: enter your domain, add a couple of competitors, get a comparative overview.
Apply the 'mentioned but not cited' filter: these are AI responses that name your brand without linking your site — your missed citation opportunities.
Apply the competitor-gap filter: queries where a competitor is mentioned and you are not.
Apply the topic-gap view: topics AI associates with a competitor instead of you.
Note all gaps before acting, because you cannot fix everything at once; these gaps feed your prioritization later.

In an ecommerce context, translate gaps into concrete work: competitors recommended in 'best X' AI answers means you need listicle/review/Reddit presence; topics you should own means content or PDP gaps.
Use the ranking of gaps to match the biggest gap to the matched priority before spending on the smaller ones.
caveats: The source specifically names Ahrefs Brand Radar; other tools may work but the workflow shown is tool-specific — verify current interface.
Gap data reflects a snapshot; re-run periodically since AI answers shift.

cards.title: The AI Filter: deciding when a keyword is a trap vs an unlinked-mention play
cards.summary: Test each target keyword by asking whether an AI overview fully answers it; informational queries that AI 'eats' should be targeted for unlinked brand mentions, not clicks.
cards.use_when: Doing keyword research for a store and deciding where to chase clicks versus where to aim for brand mention inside AI answers.
steps: Generate seed keywords and modifiers using an AI prompt. Source template: 'I'm doing keyword research for my [type of] site which makes money through [revenue model]. My target audience are [these people]. Give me 10 seed keywords that are one to two words max and five plus modifiers that'll help me surface appropriate content formats... The seeds and modifiers should not share the same words.'
Take seeds into a keyword tool's ideas report with modifiers to build a candidate list; vet on business potential, search intent and keyword difficulty.
Run each keyword through the 'AI Filter': Google the query and ask whether an AI overview fully satisfies the searcher. If yes, nobody needs to click and the keyword may be a trap.
Use the source's data to gauge risk: AI overviews appear on ~21% of keywords but ~58% of question queries; 99.9% of keywords triggering AI overviews are informational.
For informational queries AI will 'eat', don't ignore them — change the goal from earning a click to getting your brand mentioned inside the AI response.

Find those queries via the AI-platform 'others only' filter (queries where competitors are mentioned but you aren't), then filter for best, top, versus, review, alternative to build your mention-opportunity short list.
For ecommerce especially, reserve click-earning effort for commercial/product queries and use informational queries to earn unlinked brand mentions.
caveats: The percentage figures are from the source's cited research, not guarantees for your niche.
'Trap' is a heuristic judgment, not a formula; validate against your own conversion data.

cards.title: BLUF writing for AI and human parsing
cards.summary: Bottom Line Up Front: start every section with the answer, because both people and LLMs weight the beginning and end of a passage more heavily than the middle.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting PDP copy, category intros, buying guides or FAQ blocks so AI can extract your answer cleanly.
steps: Put the direct answer in the first line of each paragraph or section; do not lead with backstory or buildup.
Assume the model chunks your content and cannot control where the chunks fall, so a buried key point may be missed by both AI and skim-reading shoppers.
For product pages, this means front-loading the value proposition, key spec, or fit decision (who it's for, what it replaces) rather than a brand-history intro.
For buying guides, state the recommendation or decision rule first, then support it.
Write simply and declaratively: one idea per sentence in clear subject-verb-object structure.
Apply the litmus test the source offers: if a sentence takes two reads to understand, it needs to be simplified.
Combine BLUF with the finding that length doesn't drive citation (see the format card) so you keep sections tight and front-loaded.
caveats: Applies to every section, not just the page intro; the source stresses beginning AND end of passages weigh more than the middle.

cards.title: Atomic content and entity-rich writing for chunk extraction
cards.summary: Make each section understandable out of context and pack it with specific entities and relationships so AI can extract and connect meaning.
cards.use_when: Structuring PDP sections, feature blocks, comparison pages or guides that AI may pull as isolated fragments.
steps: Edit every H2/section so it makes complete sense if extracted alone; AI chunks pages and you cannot control the cut points.
Avoid section openers that depend on preceding context ('as mentioned above', 'this tool'). Name the product or entity explicitly in each section.

Write entity-rich: instead of 'This tool helps with SEO', write 'Ahrefs Keywords Explorer helps you find keywords with low difficulty and high traffic potential' — more specific entities and relationships give AI more to work with.
Translate to ecommerce: instead of 'great battery life', name the exact spec, compatible models, materials and use cases so the fragment carries meaning.
Keep sentences simple and declarative with one idea per sentence, since complex sentences risk being misparsed when chunked.
Reuse the same specific entities across your site, mentions and video so you build the consensus signal AI weighs.
caveats: Atomic structuring trades some narrative flow for extractability; balance against the reading experience for human buyers.

cards.title: Content format and freshness to get cited (length doesn't matter)
cards.summary: AI citations favor lists/comparisons and freshly updated pages, not word count; over half of cited pages are under 1,000 words.
cards.use_when: Deciding the format and update cadence for store buying guides, comparison pages and category content.
steps: Drop the assumption that longer ranks: analysis of 174,000 pages cited in AI overviews showed near-zero correlation between word count and citation, and over half of cited pages were under 1,000 words.

Prioritize formats AI can pull recommendations from: 43.8% of ChatGPT-cited pages were lists — 'best X', 'top X', comparisons and reviews. For ecommerce this maps to 'best [product type]', 'X vs Y', and review/comparison content.
Treat freshness as high-leverage: for ChatGPT, 89.7% of top cited pages were updated in 2025 and 76% were refreshed within the last 30 days.
Set a refresh cadence — the source warns content untouched for six months is already at a disadvantage.
When refreshing, update the visible date, prices, spec and recommendations rather than making cosmetic edits.
Rebuild pages that lost ranking due to becoming outdated first, as the source identifies this as a fast win.
caveats: The percentages are from the source's cited analyses and reflect those datasets, not a guarantee for your category.
Refresh frequency feasible for a large catalog will vary; prioritize high-intent pages.

cards.title: Earn brand mentions in three tiers of pages
cards.summary: Branded web mentions had the strongest correlation with AI overview visibility in a study of 75,000 brands — stronger than backlinks or domain rating — so get named on other people's pages.
cards.use_when: Planning off-site AEO work (PR, lists, community, creator) to increase how often AI recommends your store.
steps: Accept the source's core claim: in a study of 75,000 brands, branded web mentions correlated most strongly with AI overview visibility — stronger than backlinks, domain rating or referring domains.

Tier 1 — third-party editorial: industry publications, review sites (The Wirecutter, TechRadar), and listicles/comparison posts on authoritative blogs. Hardest to earn, most valuable because these are the pages AI loves to cite.

Tier 2 — user-generated content: Reddit, Quora, niche forums. The source says Reddit is one of the most frequently cited sources by ChatGPT and a foundational training source. Find threads where your product or expertise genuinely answers the question and contribute real answers; join communities and contribute regularly rather than gaming.
Tier 3 — owned properties: your YouTube channel, podcast, LinkedIn — all indexable and crawlable.
Remember consensus: the more places your brand appears in a topically relevant way, the more training examples AI has.
For ecommerce, actively pursue inclusion in 'best X' listicles and answer real buyer questions in communities rather than only owning your own pages.
caveats: The correlation figures are from the source's cited study, not causal guarantees.
Community contribution warns against gaming; genuine participation is implied as the ethical requirement.

cards.title: YouTube AEO: target search hits over viral hits
cards.summary: YouTube is the most cited domain in Google AI overviews and YouTube mentions showed the strongest correlation with ChatGPT visibility in the source's data — build evergreen search-hit videos, not viral spikes.
cards.use_when: Planning video content or creator sponsorships to increase AI visibility for your store.
steps: Prioritize YouTube because the source reports it is the most cited domain in Google's AI overviews, YouTube mentions correlated 0.737 with ChatGPT visibility, and GPT-4 was trained on over a million hours of YouTube transcripts.

Choose 'search hits' not 'viral hits': search hits get consistent Google and YouTube search traffic month after month on evergreen topics, and those are the videos AI is most likely to cite; viral videos spike then die.
Find proven search-hit topics: in Ahrefs Site Explorer, set the YouTube 'watch' subfolder and use the organic keywords report, filter for top-3 rankings, and add niche terms.

Optimize each video: put the keyword in the title and within the first couple lines of the description; add timestamps for YouTube chapters; and actually say the keyword in the video, since Google understands audio and pulls from transcripts.
Retain viewer attention, since retention supports the video ranking across many search queries.
If you don't produce video, get your brand mentioned on YouTube via sponsorships or creator outreach — a mention counts as an AI-relevant signal.
For ecommerce, target evergreen 'how to choose / best X for Y' searches relevant to your products rather than trend-chasing.
caveats: 0.737 correlation and citation claims are the source's reported figures, not promises.
The topic-finding workflow is Ahrefs-specific; verify current interface.

cards.title: Technical AEO: don't accidentally block AI crawlers
cards.summary: Check robots.txt for disallow rules against GPTBot, OAI Search Bot, ClaudeBot and Google Extended, since Cloudflare's AI-bot setting defaults to blocking GPTBot.
cards.use_when: First-step technical audit before any AEO content or mention work on your store's domain.
steps: Go to yourdomain.com/robots.txt and look for any 'Disallow' rules next to GPTBot, OAI Search Bot, ClaudeBot, or Google Extended. If present, you are blocking that AI crawler.
Treat this as the first 30-second check, because if AI can't crawl the site, your content and pages are handicapped from being mentioned.
Check Cloudflare settings specifically: its 'instruct AI bot traffic with robots.txt' feature is enabled by default, so Cloudflare-hosted sites may block AI crawlers without realizing it.
Note the source's context: about 5.9% of 140 million websites were blocking GPTBot — likely mostly inherited from old robots.txt templates.
Override inherited or default rules if you want AI crawlers to access your pages, then re-verify robots.txt.
Do this before investing in content, since blocked crawlers waste that effort.
caveats: Default settings and feature names may change; verify your host/Cloudflare's current controls.
The source frames blocking as usually accidental; deliberately blocking AI crawlers may be a legitimate choice some stores make.

cards.title: Measuring AEO: AI referral traffic, bot activity and self-reported attribution
cards.summary: Track AI referral traffic (as a directional undercount), AI citation-bot activity on your pages, and 'How did you hear about us?' survey attribution to capture otherwise-hidden AI impact.
cards.use_when: Setting up store analytics for AI-driven discovery and deciding which channels actually drive sign-ups or purchases.
steps: Accept that AI search hides much that traditional SEO measures; the source says you're not flying blind and offers three things to track.

Track AI referral traffic: clicks landing on your site from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and others. Recognize the nuance that not all platforms pass referral data properly — ChatGPT source links track but in-content links on paid accounts don't — so any number is almost certainly an undercount. Use it as a relative/directional metric, not precision.

Track AI bot activity instead of (or alongside) human clicks: monitor which citation bots hit which pages, since a bot repeatedly hitting a page suggests that page is used as a source. The source suggests Cloudflare integration, which it says works on Cloudflare's free plan.

Track self-reported attribution: add 'How did you hear about us?' to sign-up flow, checkout or as a post-purchase survey, because someone who sees your brand in ChatGPT then Googles you gets attributed to organic by analytics.

Contextualize with the source's own example: at Ahrefs, AI search traffic was just 0.5% of visits but drove 12.1% of sign-ups — 23x higher conversion rate than organic — which they'd not have known without self-reported attribution.
Set measurement up from day one, then use it to judge whether content/mention/video work is moving AI visibility.
caveats: AI referral traffic is an undercount due to inconsistent referral-data passing; do not treat as exact.
Ahrefs' 0.5%/12.1%/23x figures are a single company example, not a benchmark to expect.
Features and setup (GA4 channel, Cloudflare integration) may change — verify current interfaces.

cards.title: Building a custom AEO strategy by matching gap to priority
cards.summary: Sequence AEO work: technical check first, measurement setup, then fix the biggest brand-gap by matching gap type to the right intervention.
cards.use_when: Turning AI-visibility findings into a prioritized action plan for your store.
steps: Start with the 30-second technical check on robots.txt, because blocked crawlers handicap all other work.

Set up measurement from day one, either via an AI traffic channel in GA4 or a tool with it built in, and implement the 'How did you hear about us?' question — small but highly valuable for capturing hidden AI impact.

Review your biggest brand-gap and match it to a priority: if AI doesn't associate you with topics you should own, that's a content problem — refresh pages that used to rank but lost ranking due to becoming outdated, identified as the fastest win.
If competitors keep getting recommended and you don't, pursue mentions: get included in listicles, reviews and Reddit threads where you're absent.
If AI cites formats you don't produce (e.g. video), get on YouTube — either create your own content or contact creators to amplify your brand.
The source frames AEO as layered on top of SEO: treat SEO as the foundation, then add content, mentions, YouTube and technical setup.

Time-sensitive context from the source: AI traffic grew 9.7x in the past year, ChatGPT sent more traffic than Reddit or LinkedIn, and most businesses hadn't implemented AEO yet — an argument for starting early.
caveats: The source explicitly says this is not one-size-fits-all; prioritization depends on your own gaps.
Growth and traffic-comparison figures are the source's reported context, not forecasts.

16-AEO / answer engine optimization Goes here. A condensed primer on Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). Explains the mechanics of AI search (query fan-out, retrieval probability), running a brand gap analysis to find unlinked citations, structuring content for LLMs (BLUF, entity-rich writing), optimizing YouTube videos for AI indexation, and checking robots.txt for crawler blocks. Not here. • Traditional link building campaigns without an AI citation focus -> 15-SEO • Shopify backend configurations (inventory, taxes, shipping) -> 05-SET

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a streamlined five-step strategy for Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), focusing on how LLMs process content and how to adapt traditional SEO tactics to secure brand citations in AI responses. modules: [AEO] topics: [AEO, answer engine optimization, query fan-out, brand gap analysis, AI content parsing, technical AEO, YouTube AEO, zero-click attribution] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. AEO mechanics / understanding query fan-out (how AI breaks a single prompt into dozens of synthetic searches) and the probability factors of retrieval (consensus, freshness, and authority); brand gap analysis / using tools (like Ahrefs Brand Radar) to identify missed citation opportunities, competitor gaps, and topic gaps across AI platforms; keyword and prompt research / applying the "AI Filter" to assess if an AI overview fully satisfies a query (informational intent), requiring a shift from attempting to earn a click to attempting to earn an unlinked brand mention; content creation / optimizing for AI parsing using the BLUF principle (Bottom Line Up Front), atomic content structures (making every section understandable out of context), entity-rich writing, and utilizing listicle formats; earning mentions / targeting Tier 1 editorial listicles, Tier 2 UGC (Reddit), and Tier 3 owned properties; YouTube AEO / targeting "search hits" over "viral hits," optimizing titles and timestamps, and explicitly saying the keyword in the audio, as YouTube transcripts heavily feed models like GPT-4; technical AEO / checking robots.txt to ensure crawlers like GPTBot, OAI Search Bot, ClaudeBot, and Google Extended are not blocked (especially overriding Cloudflare defaults); measuring AEO / setting up custom GA4 regex channels for AI referral domains, monitoring AI citation bots via Cloudflare logs, and capturing zero-click AI attribution via "How did you hear about us?" post-purchase surveys.

Look for.

Query Fan-Out: The concept that AI search engines break down a single user prompt into dozens of long-tail synthetic sub-queries to build a comprehensive answer (e.g., a query about a phone case generated 420 backend searches).

The BLUF Framework (Bottom Line Up Front): Writing content that places the direct answer at the very beginning of the paragraph or section, as LLMs weigh the beginning and end of passages more heavily than the middle when chunking data.

Atomic Content Structuring: Editing every H2 section so it makes complete sense out of context, anticipating that AI models will chunk and extract isolated fragments of the page during retrieval.

The Cloudflare Technical Block: Checking the robots.txt file to ensure the site isn't accidentally blocking AI crawlers, noting that Cloudflare's "instruct AI bot traffic" setting defaults to blocking GPTBot.

Self-Reported Attribution: Adding a "How did you hear about us?" post-purchase survey to capture brand awareness generated by unlinked AI mentions that otherwise show up as "Direct" or "Organic" traffic in traditional analytics.

Skip. Plugs for Ahrefs Brand Radar or Web Analytics if they are purely promotional, and generic explanations of what an AI chatbot is.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (traditional SEO), 90% growth (advanced AEO and Generative Engine Optimization tactics). Volume. ~400 words.

Why is it that AI assistants recommend some brands but completely ignore [music] others? I'll tell you this, the difference between these two groups isn't luck. The group that's winning knows the techniques and follows a strategy. The same techniques and strategy [music] that I teach in our full 1 and 1/2 hour course on answer engine optimization or AEO. But here's the thing, you don't need to watch all of it to start getting results. So, I've extracted the 80% that matters most and packed it into this video where you'll learn the five pieces to AEO to start gaining visibility in AI search. By the end of this video, you'll have your own custom AI SEO strategy for your brand. And it all starts with understanding how AI search works. Now, most people assume AI assistants work like Google. You ask questions, you get answers from a list. But it doesn't work like that. [music] When you ask an AI assistant a question, that one prompt gets fanned out into dozens of smaller, more specific searches [music] behind the scenes. This is called query fan. For example, if someone asks, "Plan me a five-day [music] trip to Japan in November." The AI doesn't just search for that and send you some results like [music] a search engine might. Instead, it breaks that prompt down into things like, "Best neighborhoods to stay in Tokyo." "November weather in Kyoto." "Is [music] the Japan Rail Pass worth it?" And then it runs it all at the same time. Then it gathers information from multiple sources and synthesizes it into a response. And to give you an idea of how deep this research can go, it was reported that ChatGPT's deep research mode ran 420 searches for a single prompt about buying a red phone case. So, if your content only ranks for the main keyword someone might type into Google, you're [music] missing the majority of the queries AI is actually using to build its answer. To get cited, you need to be relevant across an entire topic, not just one or two keywords. But here's the good news. There are patterns in what AI sites more often. And based on H refs research, three things drive that probability. First is consensus, meaning the more places your brand shows up saying the same thing about you, the more likely AI is to believe and repeat it. Second is freshness. Content cited by AI is on average 25.7% [music] fresher than what ranks in traditional Google results, meaning AI actively [music] prefers recent content. And third is authority. 76% of AI overview citations come from pages already ranking in Google's top [music] 10, which supports that traditional SEO is the foundation of AI SEO. So, if you're already ranking well in Google, you have a massive head start. Now, understanding how the game works doesn't tell you how to get results. [music] So, the next piece of the puzzle is to understand where you stand compared to your competitors. And that's done through a brand gap analysis. This is when you measure where your brand should be showing up versus where it actually is showing up across Google, AI results, and the web in general. The easiest way to do this is an H refs brand radar. Just enter your domain, add a couple of competitors, and you'll get a high-level overview of how you stand compared to your competitors. Now, the real power comes in when you apply some filters, which will expose [music] the gaps in your brand analysis. For example, you can filter for responses that mention your brand but don't cite your website. These are your missed citation opportunities. You can add a [music] competitor and filter for queries where they're mentioned but you're not. That's a competitor gap. Or, you can look at specific topics to see whether AI associates them [music] with your brand or someone else's. That's a topic gap. Now, you can't fix everything at once, so take note of these gaps because they're going to be critical when we put together your custom AEO [music] strategy in a few minutes. But before we get there, you need to understand the full [music] picture. So the next thing we need to do is keyword and prompt research. People don't search AI assistants in keywords like they do with traditional search. [music] They use prompts. But here's the good news. A lot of what you already know from SEO is directly [music] applicable to AEO, especially with Google AI overviews. You still need seed keywords to build the foundation of your research, [music] and you need modifiers to turn those seeds into real searches. Now, the fastest way to come up with both is to ask your AI assistant of choice using this exact [music] prompt. "I'm doing keyword research for my type of site which makes money through this revenue model. My target audience are these people. Give me 10 seed keywords that are one to two words max and five plus modifiers that'll help me surface appropriate content formats that I can use in my keyword research. The seeds and modifiers should not share the same words." [music] After it's done generating, take those seeds into a keyword ideas report using your favorite keyword research tool. Mine's obviously Ahrefs Keywords Explorer. Set some modifiers and you'll get a complete [music] list of keywords to potentially target. Now, beyond the usual vetting tasks like understanding business potential, search intent, and keyword difficulty, there's one more filter that you need to run every keyword through. I call it the AI filter, and it lives [music] in there. When you Google a query, ask yourself, can AI fully satisfy the searcher with an AI overview? Because even if a keyword is great on paper, if Google's AI overview answers it so well that nobody needs to click through, that keyword might be a trap. And there's hard data behind this. AI overviews [music] appear on about 21% of all keywords, but nearly 58% of question queries trigger them. And get this, 99.9% of keywords that trigger AI overviews >> [music] >> are informational in intent. So, for those informational queries where AI is clearly going to eat the click, you don't ignore them. You got to target them differently. Instead of trying to rank and earn a click, your goal is to get your brand mentioned inside the [music] AI response itself. Now, to find those queries, head back to Brand Radar, hover over the AI platform you want to research, and click [music] others only. This shows you queries where competitors are getting mentioned, but you're not. Filter for best, top, versus, review, alternative, and you've got your short list of brand mention opportunities to go after. Okay, so now you know how the game works. You know where you stand, and you know which topics and prompts to target. Now, it's time to actually close those gaps, and much of that comes down to getting cited. Citations in AI search boils down to four things: your content, your mentions, your YouTube presence, and your technical setup. Let's talk about content on your own site first. So, I was digging through our research, and I found a few key data points that hint at how to create content that gets cited by AI. First is that content length doesn't matter. We analyzed 174,000 pages cited in AI overviews, and the correlation between word count and getting cited is basically zero. Over half of all cited pages are under 1,000 words. So, if you've been writing 3,000 word articles thinking longer is better, that doesn't apply here. On the other hand, freshness matters a lot. For ChatGPT specifically, 89.7% of its top cited pages were updated in 2025. And get this, 76% were refreshed within the last 30 days. So, if your content hasn't been touched in 6 months, you're already at a disadvantage. And third, format matters. 43.8% of all pages cited by ChatGPT are lists, best X, top X, comparisons and reviews. This is not some weird coincidence. These formats give AI structured and clear recommendations that it can pull from. Now, that's the macro approach to content creation. Keep your content focused, fresh, and use formats that AI can actually use. The micro approach on the other hand comes down to how you structure your content. And there are four principles [music] to follow. So, first is bluff, which stands for bottom line up front. This means that you should start every section with the answer, not the backstory. Both humans and AI weigh the beginning and end of a passage more heavily [music] than the middle. So, if your key point is buried three paragraphs in, both might miss it. Second is to create atomic content. [music] Basically, every section on your page should be able to stand on its own. And that's because AI chunks your content into pieces [music] when it processes it, and you can't control where the chunks fall. So, ideally, you want [music] every section to make sense out of context so the meaning survives no matter how AI pulls it. Third is entity rich writing. Instead of "This tool helps with SEO", write [music] "Ahrefs Keywords Explorer helps you find keywords with low difficulty and high traffic potential." The more specific entities and relationships in your writing, the more AI [music] actually has to work with to piece together relationships. And fourth, [music] keep your content simple and declarative. Write one idea per sentence in clear subject-verb-object structure. A good litmus test is that if a sentence takes two reads to understand, it's too complex and it [music] needs to be simplified. Now, great content on your own site is half the equation because here's the thing, a lot of AEO isn't about what's on your site, it's about getting mentioned on other people's pages. And this is where things get really [music] interesting. In a study of 75,000 brands, branded web mentions have the strongest correlation with visibility in AI overviews. That's stronger than backlinks, domain rating, referring domains, or anything else that we studied, which means [music] the single highest leverage thing you can do for AI visibility is get your brand named on other people's pages. And there are three tiers of pages to focus [music] on. Tier one are third-party editorial sites. This can be industry publications, review sites like The Wirecutter or TechRadar, and listicles and comparison posts on authoritative blogs. These are the hardest mentions to earn, but they're also the most valuable because they're exactly the kinds of pages that AI loves to cite. Tier two is user-generated content, and this can be in [music] community platforms like Reddit, Quora, or niche forums. Reddit is actually one of the most frequently cited sources by ChatGPT, and it's a foundational training source for large language models. So, find threads where people are asking questions that your product or expertise can genuinely answer, and contribute real answers. And don't just stop there. Go and join other communities where you can contribute regularly to. The idea isn't to game the system, it's to interact with your target audience. And tier three is your [music] own properties, like your YouTube channel, your podcast, your LinkedIn content. They're all indexed and accessible [music] to crawlers, so they can all potentially be sources AI pulls from. And remember, AI looks at consensus, so the more places your brand appears in a topically relevant way, the more training examples AI has to [music] learn from. Now, of those three tiers, there's one specific platform that deserves its own conversation because the data on this one is honestly kind of crazy, and that's YouTube. YouTube is the most cited domain in Google's AI overviews. And get this, YouTube mentions have a 0.737 correlation with ChatGPT visibility. That is the strongest correlation of any factor we studied. And there's a reason for that. GPT-4 was trained on over a million hours of YouTube transcripts. So, YouTube isn't just a platform that [music] AI sites, it's a platform AI has learned from, which means that if you want to dramatically increase your AI visibility, getting your brand mentioned on YouTube is one of the highest impact moves [music] you can make. And you can do this through sponsorships, outreach, or my favorite way, create YouTube search hits. You see, most people on YouTube target viral hits. And the videos usually start off strong with a big spike, [music] but once the YouTube algorithm has exhausted that interested audience, or if the video doesn't quite land like you'd hope it does, it dies, and it dies fast. A search hit, on the other hand, gets you consistent traffic from both Google and YouTube search, month after month, because people are actively searching for these evergreen topics. And those are exactly the videos AI is most likely to cite. To find topics that are proven search hits, you can look at the organic keywords report in Ahrefs Site Explorer with YouTube's [music] watch subfolder set. Filter for keywords ranking in the top three, and add terms related to your [music] niche. And now you have a list of potential search topics. Then just make the video and follow this exact video SEO optimization checklist. Put the keyword in the title and within the first couple lines of the description. Add timestamps for YouTube chapters, and actually [music] say the keyword in the video, because Google understands audio and pulls from it. Now, if you can retain the audience's attention, your video has a great chance of showing up every time for various search queries. Now, content mentions in YouTube cover most of what you'll spend time on in your AEO efforts, but there's something important we haven't covered yet [music] that's actually more about what not to do and that's to not accidentally block AI crawlers. According to our data, about 5.9% of 140 million websites are blocking GPTBot, which is OpenAI's crawler. That's millions of sites that are asking [music] ChatGPT not to view their pages. Now, in these people's defense, I'm guessing that most of them didn't do it on purpose. A lot of sites inherit robots.txt rules from old templates. In fact, if your site is on Cloudflare, you could be blocking AI crawlers without realizing it. And that's because they have a feature called instruct AI bot traffic with robots.txt that's now enabled by default. To check if your site is blocking AI crawlers, go to your domain.com/robots.txt and look for any disallow rules next to GPTBot, OAI search bot, ClaudeBot, or Google extended. If you see any, you're blocking that AI crawler from your site. All right, so now you've got the playbook: content, mentions, YouTube, [music] and technical. That's four pieces of the puzzle down. But none of this matters if you can't tell whether it's working. And that brings us to the next essential, which is to measure what's working. Now, I'm going to be up front with you. With traditional SEO, you've got Google Search Console giving you impressions, clicks, and rankings. With AI search, a lot of that data either doesn't exist or it's hidden from you. But you're not flying blind because there are three things you can track and together they give you a pretty clear picture of what's happening with your brand in AI. The first is AI referral traffic. This is when someone clicks through from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, or any other AI platform and lands on your site. Now, it's important to know that there are nuances that come with tracking because not all AI platforms pass referral data properly. For example, ChatGPT's source links track properly, but in-content links on paid accounts don't. So, that means that whatever number you see in your analytics is almost certainly an undercount. So, it's useful for direction and as a relative metric, but not for precision. If you don't know how to set up this type of tracking in GA4, we have a video on that in our AEO course, so I'll link that up for you. Or, you can skip the install with GA4 [music] and install Ahrefs Web Analytics, which already has that and many other features built in and it's completely free. Now, the second thing to track is AI bot activity on your site. Instead of tracking the humans clicking through, we track the bots that visit your pages to read and index your content. And that's because if a citation bot keeps hitting a specific page, that page is likely being used as a source [music] in AI responses. The easiest way to track this is with a Cloudflare integration in Ahrefs Web Analytics, which works on Cloudflare's free plan. And the third thing to track is self-reported attribution. This one's probably the [music] least used method, but it might be the most important because a lot of the impact of AI visibility doesn't show up in your analytics at all. For example, if someone asks ChatGPT for a recommendation, they might see our brand name and Google it afterwards, but analytics tools are going to attribute that conversion to organic. So, in my opinion, attribution is the most meaningful when it comes from the perspective of [music] the customer. So, add a simple question like, "How'd you hear about us?" to your sign-up flow, to your checkout, or as a post-purchase survey. Now, to put this into perspective at Ahrefs, AI search traffic was just 0.5% of our visits, but it drove 12.1% of our sign-ups. That's a 23 times higher conversion rate than organic search. And we would have never known that without self-reported attributions. Now, the brands winning in AI search, they aren't doing anything magical. They're treating SEO as the foundation, then they're layering AEO or AI SEO, whatever you want to call it, on top of it. They're adding content, mentions, YouTube, and the technical setup. That's it. But, this isn't a one-size-fits-all approach here. So, here's how you can turn this into your own customized AEO strategy. Start with the 30-second technical check we covered because if AI can't crawl your site, you're handicapping your content and your pages from being mentioned. Then, [music] set up your measurements from day one, either with HS web analytics or the AI traffic channel in GA4. >> [music] >> Also, implement the how did you hear about us question. I know it's small, >> [music] >> but it can be really, really valuable. Next, look at the biggest gap you noted from your brand gap analysis and match it to your priorities. For [music] example, if AI doesn't associate you with topics you should own, that's a content problem. Start by refreshing pages that used to rank but lost its ranking due to becoming outdated. This will be your fastest win. Or if competitors keep getting recommended by AI and you're not, then look at getting mentioned in listicles, reviews, [music] and Reddit threads where you aren't a part of that conversation. And if AI is citing content [music] formats you don't produce, like videos, you need to get on YouTube, whether that's creating your own content or getting in touch with creators that can amplify your brand. Now, the reason to do this now is that AI traffic has grown 9.7 times in the past year. >> [music] >> ChatGPT alone has grown 85% since January and now sends more traffic than Reddit or LinkedIn. But, most businesses haven't even started implementing AEO into their marketing strategy. So, it's worth getting started before [music] everyone else does to get a head start. And if you want the full playbook with every workflow, watch our complete AEO course [music] for beginners, which is right here on our channel.
